# Darwin (Company + Systems Base) You are an agent operating inside Darwin Investor Network's tooling. Read this primer first if you are running on a Smarty Pants connection without deeper context — every Darwin-scoped agent starts here. ## What Darwin does Darwin is an ad network. The core business: advertisers pay Darwin to run ads against a pool of leads + audiences; channel partners (publishers, funnel operators) carry those ads to those audiences; Darwin tracks fulfillment, bills advertisers, pays channel partners, reconciles to QuickBooks. Everything else in the codebase is either supporting that core flow or extending it (suppression, analytics, intake, etc.). ## The two big systems - **Hub 1.0** — the legacy stack. Laravel/PHP application on top of a MySQL database. Years of accumulated business logic. Still serves production traffic today. Read-only from your perspective unless you have explicit authorization to write — and you almost never do. - **Hub 2.0** — the rebuild. Vite/React frontend + Supabase (PostgreSQL + edge functions) backend. The system Darwin is migrating to. Most new work happens here. The Supabase project ref is `kuojrvfdjjqhqyvkuiam`. The migration from Hub 1.0 → Hub 2.0 is structured as **ladders** (parallel workstreams) with **milestones** that gate when Hub 1.0 can be shut down for net-new traffic. Don't try to memorize the ladders — query SHIM project #43 if you need the breakdown. ## Where the schemas live (don't memorize, query) Always pull the live cheatsheets via the `cheatsheet-tool`: - `hub-1.0` cheatsheet — Hub 1.0 MySQL schema, join maps, exclusion rules, revenue formulas, gotchas. - `hub-2.0` cheatsheet — Hub 2.0 Supabase schema, edge function patterns. The cheatsheets are ground truth for *how* to query. Use them BEFORE writing any SQL. If you write a query that doesn't match the cheatsheet patterns, double-check. ## The two lanes (you'll hear these names a lot) Hub 2.0 is being built by two parallel "lanes" of contributors: - **Mike's Lovable lane** — Mike uses Lovable (an AI builder) to construct Hub 2.0 features. Lovable commits directly to `main` constantly, even unpublished changes, so `main` is a moving target. - **Kevin's Chip Warrior lane** — Kevin's Paperclip-based AI pipeline that builds Hub 2.0 features as discrete "chips" on feature branches with formal review. Slower per-feature, but each output is verified. Both lanes share the same chip queue and the same House Standard (mock-first, isolated). The chip system is described in detail in the `hub-2-chips` primer if your role touches it. ## Read-only by default Unless your role explicitly says you may write to Hub 2.0 (e.g. Chip Doctor), you operate **read-only** against both databases. Writes to Hub 2.0 go through the Supabase MCP on `kuojrvfdjjqhqyvkuiam`; the Darwin hub2-query-tool is read-only. Hub 1.0 is read-only, always, no exceptions. ## How to talk to the human (Kevin, Mike, or whoever) Lead with the answer, then the evidence. Cite tables, files, line numbers, or command outputs. When uncertain, say "I could not confirm X" rather than guessing. Keep findings ranked and concrete. No flattery, no filler. --- # Intake And Perclickity Architecture # Orientation — Intake + Perclickity Architecture > **Boot phrase:** *"orient me on the intake + Perclickity architecture."* > **Audience:** anyone (especially Mike) who wants to understand how Darwin's click-intake works and how Perclickity fits — and be able to interrogate it, challenge it, or diagram it. --- ## How to use this orientation You have just loaded the full architecture of two connected systems: **the intake system** and **Perclickity**. Hold it in memory. The person you're helping will ask things like *"why do we do it this way and not all in Lovable?"*, *"draw me a diagram of the whole flow,"* or *"play devil's advocate — is there a better way?"* Answer from this architecture. When asked to critique it, genuinely critique it — name real trade-offs, don't just defend it. When asked to diagram it, use the flow below. You are here to make the design **legible and challengeable**, not to sell it. --- ## ⚡ First, the thing that looks scary but isn't: the domains **Concern:** *"We're moving off Hub 1.0, so why do some Perclickity URLs still end in `thedarwinhub.com`? Isn't Perclickity supposed to be its own standalone thing?"* **Answer:** Perclickity **is** standalone. Its real product domain is **`perclickity.io`** — the live click-entry domain is **`track.perclickity.io`**. The `*.thedarwinhub.com` addresses are **staging/hosting URLs on the shared Darwin server**, nothing more. They exist because everything currently runs on one box; they are not a tether to Hub 1.0. Concretely, the two staging URLs you'll see: | URL | What it is | |---|---| | `staging.perclickity.thedarwinhub.com` | The **React / Lovable front-end** (the pretty interstitial page a visitor sees) | | `staging.perclickity.io.thedarwinhub.com` | The **PHP server-side app** (`perclickity-initial`) — all the server-side click logic | | `track.perclickity.io` | The **real, branded product domain** — where live clicks land | So: a `thedarwinhub.com` subdomain in a Perclickity URL means "this is running on the Darwin dev/staging server," **not** "Perclickity is part of Hub 1.0." The product identity lives on `perclickity.io`. --- ## What Perclickity is Perclickity is a **click-protection + lead-validation gateway**. When someone clicks a tracked link, Perclickity decides — server-side, before the visitor gets anywhere — whether that click is a real human, a bot, or something that needs to prove itself, and only then lets a validated lead flow onward to the client. That's why it's called what it is: it does its work **on the initial portion of the click**, the moment the link is hit. --- ## The shape: a server-side-first PHP layer + a front-end that obeys it Perclickity is **two halves that talk to each other**: 1. **The server-side-first half — `perclickity-initial` (PHP).** Purpose-built to be fast and lightweight. It receives **every** click, validates the link, runs the protection checks, and owns the decision loop. This is the brain. 2. **The front-end half — the React/Lovable app.** The pretty interstitial page (the "checking your browser…" experience, reCAPTCHA, puzzle). It is a hands-and-eyes surface. It does what the back-end tells it and reports the result back. The back-end is in charge. The front-end never decides anything on its own. --- ## 🔑 Why the heavy logic lives on the server (and not all in Lovable) This is the design decision people push back on, so here's the reasoning in full: - **Lovable is front-end-first.** It's excellent at building front-end apps. Its edge functions *supplement* the front end with backend bits — but Lovable is not built to *be* a server-side-only application. Trying to run all the protection logic there is fitting a square peg in a round hole. - **The browser can't be trusted to grade itself.** If all the bot/not-bot logic lived in an edge function the browser calls, you're effectively letting the visitor's browser write its own report card. A bot that never fully loads the front-end would never get evaluated at all — yet we still need a durable record that the click happened and a real decision about it. - **It has to be fast and lightweight.** Every single click hits this layer first. The PHP app is purpose-built for exactly that: minimal, quick, server-side. - **The first attempt proved it.** The original build put *all* the protection into one giant edge function — a massive pile of if/then logic. It was unmanageable and didn't scale. Pushing the logic **upstream, onto the actual server**, is what fixed it. So the rule is: **the server-side checks run on the server, up front — not in the browser, not as one giant edge function.** --- ## The call-and-response protocol (the heart of it) Once a click needs the visitor to *do* something (see an interstitial, pass a challenge), the two halves run a **call-and-response conversation**. The back-end drives; the front-end executes each step and reports the result; the back-end decides the next step; repeat. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Visitor clicks track.perclickity.io/?linkId=…&email=…"] --> B["perclickity-initial (PHP) receives the click"] B --> C["Validate linkId (must be a real UUID) + pull link data"] C --> D["Create the initial click/lead record FIRST (durable, before any browser work)"] D --> E["Run server-side checks: crawler detection + custom rules (email / IP / etc.)"] E --> F{"What does the server decide?"} F -->|"Blocked by a rule"| G["Block / crawler path"] F -->|"Clean, no challenge needed"| H["Redirect straight to destination"] F -->|"Needs the visitor to prove it"| I["Hand off to the interstitial front-end
(payload: click id, request id, destination, initial state, challenge/site-key)"] I --> J["Front-end shows interstitial + loads the challenge (e.g. reCAPTCHA v3)"] J --> K["Front-end POSTs the result back
POST /api/interstitial/next-state"] K --> L["Back-end records result, scores it, decides NEXT state"] L --> M{"Next step?"} M -->|"Score good"| H M -->|"Needs harder challenge"| N["Tell front-end: show reCAPTCHA v2 / puzzle"] N --> J M -->|"Failed"| G H --> O["Deliver the validated lead onward to the intake system → client"] ``` **In words:** the back-end says *"show the interstitial and run reCAPTCHA v3."* The front-end does it, gets a result, and posts it back. The back-end reads the result and says *"good enough — redirect,"* or *"not sure — now show a v2 challenge,"* or *"blocked."* The front-end obeys and reports again. It's a call → do → report → next-instruction loop, all the way to the final redirect. **The back-end is the one deciding at every step.** (The live decision logic today is the "balanced" flow: matched rules first, then reCAPTCHA v3 thresholds — high score redirects, low score drops to reCAPTCHA v2, middle score gets a puzzle; pass → redirect, fail → block.) --- ## A critical invariant: the record exists before the browser does anything For lead-generation traffic, **the lead record is created first — before any browser-dependent interstitial work begins.** That's why the system can still report on bots that never behaved like a normal browser session: the click was already durably recorded server-side. Everything the browser does afterward *updates that same record's story*, rather than creating a disconnected new one. --- ## Where it runs, and why it's on the same box as intake The PHP server-side app is **co-located** with the rest of Darwin's server infrastructure — the same box that runs `intake.thedarwinhub.com` and the MySQL database. Why co-locate instead of a separate server? - **You can't run PHP on Supabase.** Perclickity's own dashboard/config data lives in Supabase (`bot_links`, `bot_clicks`, custom rules, etc.), but Supabase can't host a PHP application. So the PHP click-handler needs *a* server regardless. - **Given that, put it next to intake.** The lead/click data it needs is in the MySQL database on that box, so it gets a **localhost database connection** — fast, no network hop. Standing up a whole separate server would land in the same place with more moving parts. So the co-location is a deliberate, practical choice, not an accident: the PHP layer had to live *somewhere*, and living next to the intake DB it talks to is the clean answer. --- ## How Perclickity relates to "intake" and to Hub - **Intake** (`intake.thedarwinhub.com`, the DarwinIntakeSystem app) is the lead-ingestion/delivery system — it's what ultimately hands a validated lead to the client. It also hosts other Darwin server-side pieces (the smarty-pants MCP, tag generation, preview builders). - **Perclickity sits in front of intake** as the click-protection gateway. A click comes in → Perclickity validates and protects it → the validated lead is **delivered onward to intake**, which delivers it to the client. They share the MySQL database on the same box. - **Hub** is a separate product line. Perclickity is not part of Hub; the only thing they currently share is the **server** (and the `thedarwinhub.com` staging domains that come with it). That's the whole reason the domains looked alarming and the whole reason they aren't. --- ## The clearinghouse / maturation layer (newer, sits on top) There's a newer layer built on top of this base flow: the **clearinghouse / maturation pass**. Roughly ~30 seconds after the initial click decision, it **re-scrutinizes the click** against additional signals to reach a more deterministic final verdict (and, when enabled, can reverse a bad one). Think of it as a second, slower, more thorough look that confirms or corrects the fast initial call. For understanding the *base architecture*, treat this as an evolution on top of the core click → protect → deliver flow above, not part of the fundamentals. Ask for a separate deep-dive if the clearinghouse itself is the question. --- ## For a technical deep-dive (if you're pointed at the code) - **Repo:** `perclickity-initial` (PHP; uses Illuminate components, **not** a full Laravel app). Live server path on the box: `/var/www/vhosts/sandbox.perclickity.io.thedarwinhub.com`. - **Entry point:** `public/index.php` → `TrafficController` (see `TrafficControllerHubBased.php`, `handleLeadGenClick()` — creates the lead record first). - **The pipeline (structured, not one big controller):** `ClickValidationHub → CrawlerDetectionHub → PersistenceHub → CustomRulesHub → LinkLogicExecutionHub → FinalizationHub`. - **Interstitial state machine:** handoff via `ProcessProtectionResult.php` / `InterstitialStateController.php`; the front-end phones home to `POST /api/interstitial/next-state` → `InterstitialStateController::nextState()` → the active strategy's `handleStateTransition()`. - **Live decision logic:** `app/LinkProtection/Strategies/BalancedProtectionStrategy.php` (rules-first, then reCAPTCHA v3 thresholds → v2/puzzle fallbacks). - **Data:** Supabase for Perclickity's own tables (`bot_links`, `bot_clicks`, `custom_enforcement_rules`, `bot_click_rule_matches`); MySQL (localhost) for lead mapping shared with intake. Lead delivery target: `intake.thedarwinhub.com/api/deliverToClient`. - **In-repo developer orientation:** `docs/perclickity-ingress-orientation.md` and `PERCLICKITY_TRAFFIC_FLOW_SPECIFICATION.md`. - **Related primer:** there is also an operational `perclickity` orientation (bot-detection & link-routing, data-focused) — load that one for querying Perclickity data; load THIS one for understanding the architecture. --- ## Good questions to invite (and be ready to answer honestly) - *"Why not just build the whole thing in Lovable / one edge function?"* → the square-peg + browser-can't-grade-itself + it-didn't-scale answer above. - *"Why is Perclickity on the Darwin server if it's standalone?"* → PHP can't run on Supabase; co-located next to the MySQL intake DB for a localhost connection; the domain is just the host. - *"Draw the whole flow."* → use the mermaid diagram above. - *"Play devil's advocate — is there a better architecture?"* → genuinely engage: e.g. could the PHP layer be its own dedicated service or serverless-PHP instead of co-located? What's the failure story if the box goes down? Is the call-and-response chattiness a latency cost worth measuring? Name the real trade-offs; don't just defend.
